sheet.howExamined: B1, 1 hour, calculator allowed: 60 marks at Foundation, 70 at Higher. Enzymes take a whole question of 6 to 9 marks, usually with a lock and key diagram and a word list. The marks come as [1] lines: name the type of molecule, give the letter of the substrate, two terms per molecule, name the enzyme for a named food, and a [2] or [3] explanation of why digestion is necessary. Most series also put an enzyme context inside the 6-mark QWC. The listing rule applies to every 'give the letter' part, and the schemes reject near-miss words such as 'site' for 'active site' or 'lipid' for 'lipase'.
traps: Naming the molecule going in as the product rather than the substrate (Summer 2025 B1 F Q5(b))
Giving only one of the two terms asked for — the job without the name, or the other way round
Mixing rows: protease producing fatty acids, or amylase producing amino acids
Leaving out 'without being used up' from the definition of a catalyst
Explaining specificity as denaturation — nothing has gone wrong with the enzyme
Two letters written on a one-letter answer line, which loses the mark under the listing rule
Writing everything known about enzymes instead of answering the question asked (Summer 2023 B1 F Q7(d) and B1 H Q2(d))

noteBlocks.lede: Enzymes are proteins that speed reactions up without being used up. Each has an active site shaped to fit one substrate, which is why you need a different enzyme for starch, protein and fat. Digestion is that idea at work, turning food into molecules small enough to absorb.

Explain why large insoluble food molecules have to be broken down.

noteBlocks.text: Enzymes, the lock and key, and digestion

noteBlocks.md: An enzyme is a protein with a dent in it shaped to fit one particular molecule. Your gut is full of them, taking food apart fast enough to be absorbed, and the same proteins lift egg and grease out of a shirt at 40 °C.

noteBlocks.alt: Three stages. First, a substrate made of two joined parts sits above an enzyme with a notch-shaped active site of the matching shape. Second, the substrate is in the active site, forming the enzyme-substrate complex. Third, the two products have separated and left, and the enzyme is unchanged with its active site empty.

noteBlocks.md: An enzyme is a **protein** that acts as a **biological catalyst**: it speeds up the rate of a reaction **without being used up**. That last clause is a marking point of its own — the enzyme is still there at the end, ready for the next molecule, which is why a cell needs so little of it.

noteBlocks.prompt: Enzymes are made of which type of molecule?
noteBlocks.explain: Protein — which is why heat and pH can wreck them, as you will see in the next topic.

noteBlocks.md: **The lock and key model.** The enzyme has a dent in it called the **active site**. The **substrate** — the molecule the enzyme works on — has a shape **complementary** to that active site, so it fits in. While it is there the reaction happens, and the **products** leave. The enzyme is unchanged and does it all again.

noteBlocks.prompt: The part of an enzyme that the substrate fits into is called the ______ ______ .
noteBlocks.explain: The active site. Both words are needed; 'site' on its own is not credited, and neither is 'the dent'.

noteBlocks.title: Why the shape matters so much
noteBlocks.md: The fit is what makes the reaction happen, and it is also what makes each enzyme **specific**. If the substrate's shape does not match the active site, nothing happens at all — the enzyme simply ignores it. That is why you need a different enzyme for starch, for protein and for fat, rather than one all-purpose one.

noteBlocks.alt: One enzyme with a notch-shaped active site, drawn beside three possible substrate molecules: A has the matching notch shape, B is a rectangle and C is a circle. Only A can fit.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 720 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="e62t"><title id="e62t">One enzyme and three possible substrate molecules, only one of which has a shape complementary to the active site</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"><path d="M40 200 H160 V126 H132 L120 148 H80 L68 126 H40 Z"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"><path d="M280 60 H352 L336 102 H296 Z"/><rect x="440" y="60" width="70" height="42" rx="6"/><circle cx="606" cy="81" r="24"/></g><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="30" font-weight="600">One enzyme</text><text x="270" y="30" font-weight="600">Three possible substrates</text><text x="300" y="132">A</text><text x="470" y="132">B</text><text x="600" y="132">C</text><text x="20" y="232">Only A has a shape complementary to this active site, so only A can be broken down by this enzyme.</text><text x="20" y="248" font-size="11.5">That is what substrate specificity means: one enzyme, one job.</text><text x="166" y="150">active site</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: Substrate specificity: only A fits, so only A is broken down.

noteBlocks.prompt: Look at the figure. Which molecule is the substrate for this enzyme?
noteBlocks.explain: A, because its shape is complementary to the active site. The other two cannot enter, so the enzyme has no effect on them.

noteBlocks.alt: A table with three rows. Carbohydrase, also called amylase, works on starch and produces simple sugars such as glucose. Protease works on protein and produces amino acids. Lipase works on fat or lipid and produces fatty acids and glycerol.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 760 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="e63t"><title id="e63t">The three digestive enzymes with the substrate each one works on and the products it makes</title><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none"><path d="M20 40 h720 v160 h-720 z"/><path d="M20 78 h720 M20 118 h720 M20 158 h720"/><path d="M260 40 v160 M470 40 v160"/></g><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600"><text x="32" y="64">Enzyme</text><text x="272" y="64">Substrate (large, insoluble)</text><text x="482" y="64">Products (small, soluble)</text></g><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="32" y="104">carbohydrase (amylase)</text><text x="272" y="104">starch</text><text x="482" y="104">simple sugars (glucose)</text><text x="32" y="144">protease</text><text x="272" y="144">protein</text><text x="482" y="144">amino acids</text><text x="32" y="184">lipase</text><text x="272" y="184">fat (lipid)</text><text x="482" y="184">fatty acids and glycerol</text></g><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="28">Each enzyme is named after the substrate it works on, not the product it makes.</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: Read across, never down: each enzyme keeps its own row.

noteBlocks.md: Each one is named after **what it works on**, not what it makes. **Carbohydrase** (the one you meet is **amylase**) digests starch into simple sugars. **Protease** digests protein into amino acids. **Lipase** digests fat into fatty acids and glycerol. Three rows, and the question usually gives you one cell and asks for another.

noteBlocks.prompt: Lipase digests fat into glycerol and ______ ______ .
noteBlocks.explain: Fatty acids. Both products are wanted, so 'glycerol' alone is half an answer.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q5(b)
noteBlocks.md: A diagram showed three molecules in a lock and key reaction and asked for **two terms for each one**. Most candidates picked up some of the six marks, but the report says identifying the terms for the three molecules was difficult. The fix is mechanical: for each molecule ask 'what is its **job** here — enzyme, substrate or product?' and then 'what is its **name** — lipase, fat, glycerol?' Two answers, two different kinds of answer.

noteBlocks.prompt: Lipase breaks fat into fatty acids and glycerol. Which of the three is the substrate?
noteBlocks.explain: Fat. Lipase is the enzyme and glycerol is one of the products.

noteBlocks.text: Why digestion needs them at all

noteBlocks.alt: A large insoluble molecule drawn as four joined circles is acted on by an enzyme and becomes four separate small soluble molecules, which pass through the gut wall into the blood.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 740 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="e64t"><title id="e64t">A large insoluble molecule digested by an enzyme into small soluble molecules that pass through the gut wall into the blood</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><circle cx="70" cy="120" r="16"/><circle cx="98" cy="120" r="16"/><circle cx="126" cy="120" r="16"/><circle cx="154" cy="120" r="16"/><circle cx="330" cy="102" r="13"/><circle cx="372" cy="132" r="13"/><circle cx="414" cy="100" r="13"/><circle cx="352" cy="168" r="13"/><path d="M520 40 v180" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/><path d="M600 40 v180"/><path d="M600 60 c40 20 40 60 0 80 c-40 20 -40 60 0 80"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"><path d="M188 120 h72" marker-end="url(#ab64)"/><path d="M448 120 h50" marker-end="url(#ab64)"/></g><defs><marker id="ab64" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="30" font-weight="600">Digestion</text><text x="20" y="176">large, insoluble</text><text x="20" y="192">molecule</text><text x="196" y="112">enzyme</text><text x="320" y="210">small, soluble</text><text x="320" y="226">molecules</text><text x="480" y="240">gut wall</text><text x="612" y="34">blood</text><text x="20" y="252" font-size="12">Only small soluble molecules can pass through the gut wall and be absorbed into the bloodstream.</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: Large and insoluble on the left; small, soluble and absorbed on the right.

noteBlocks.md: Food molecules arrive **large and insoluble** — too big to cross the gut wall. Enzymes break them into **small, soluble** molecules that **can be absorbed into the bloodstream**. Those four adjectives are the answer to 'why is digestion necessary', and CCEA's glossary uses exactly them.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why must large food molecules be digested?
options: They are insoluble and too large to be absorbed into the blood
They contain too much energy to be used at once
They would be attacked by bacteria in the gut
noteBlocks.answer: They are insoluble and too large to be absorbed into the blood
noteBlocks.explain: Size and solubility. The small soluble products can pass through the gut wall; the large insoluble ones cannot.

noteBlocks.md: **Outside the body.** Because enzymes work at low temperatures and break big molecules into small ones, industry uses them too. **Biological washing powders** contain protease and lipase, so they lift protein stains such as blood and egg, and grease, at 30 or 40 °C instead of a hot wash. That saves energy and money — the 'commercial and economic uses' the specification asks for.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which two enzymes would be most useful in a biological washing powder for egg and grease stains?
noteBlocks.explain: Egg is protein, so protease; grease is fat, so lipase. Naming the stain first tells you the enzyme.

noteBlocks.md:
Say what an enzyme is: a **protein** that is a **biological catalyst**, not used up.
Use **enzyme, substrate, active site** and **product** on a lock and key diagram.

Explain why digestion is needed: **large and insoluble** to **small and soluble**.

The diagram shows three stages of an enzyme reaction. Molecule V is the enzyme, W is the molecule it acts on and Z is one of the molecules released at the end. The reaction digests a fat.

enzyme · substrate · product · lipase · fat (lipid) · glycerol · amylase · amino acid [6]

steps.decision: Two kinds of answer are wanted for each molecule: the job it does, and its name. V has the active site and is unchanged at the end, so its job is enzyme. The reaction digests a fat, so its name is lipase.
W is what the enzyme acts on, so its job is substrate. The question says the reaction digests a fat, so its name is fat or lipid. Not 'fatty acid' — that is one of the things it turns into.

options: Because the substrate is what goes in, not what comes out
Because fat is the only word left
Because W is bigger than Z
whyMenu.explain: Substrate goes in; product comes out. Fat is the substrate of lipase, and fatty acids and glycerol are its products.

steps.decision: Z is released at the end, so its job is product. Lipase makes fatty acids and glycerol; glycerol is the one on the list, so that is its name.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: V: enzyme, lipase. W: substrate, fat (lipid). Z: product, glycerol.

steps.working: Protein molecules are large and insoluble.
steps.decision: Start with the property of the food, not with the enzyme. The whole reason digestion exists is the size and solubility of what arrives.

steps.working: A protease breaks the protein down into amino acids, which are small and soluble.
steps.decision: Name the enzyme and the products. 'Broken into smaller pieces' is vague; 'amino acids' is the marking point.

steps.working: The amino acids can then be absorbed through the gut wall into the bloodstream.
steps.decision: Finish with where they go. Three sentences, three marks — nothing else needed, and Summer 2023's report warns against adding it.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Protein molecules are large and insoluble, so a protease digests them into amino acids, which are small and soluble and can be absorbed through the gut wall into the bloodstream.

twin.stem: Explain why starch has to be digested before the body can use it.

accepted: starch is a large insoluble molecule, so amylase digests it into simple sugars which are small and soluble and can be absorbed into the blood

items.stem: What happens to an enzyme molecule during the reaction it catalyses?
items.skill: Recall that a catalyst is not used up

options.text: Nothing — it is unchanged and can be used again
options.feedback: That is what 'without being used up' means, and it is a separate marking point in the definition.

options.text: It is broken down into amino acids
options.feedback: Enzymes are made of amino acids, but they are not digested by the reaction they catalyse. They come out of it unchanged.

options.text: It joins to the product and leaves with it
options.feedback: The products leave on their own; the active site empties and is ready for the next substrate.

options.text: It is used up, so more must be made each time
options.feedback: If it were used up a cell would need enormous amounts of it. A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.

items.stem: Which enzyme digests protein, and what does it produce?
items.skill: Match enzyme, substrate and product across one row

options.text: protease, producing amino acids
options.feedback: Named after the substrate, as they all are. Protein in, amino acids out.

options.text: protease, producing fatty acids and glycerol
options.feedback: Fatty acids and glycerol are what lipase makes from fat. Keep each enzyme inside its own row.

options.text: amylase, producing amino acids
options.feedback: Amylase works on starch. The names are close, which is exactly why the mark is there.

options.text: lipase, producing amino acids
options.feedback: Lipase works on fat. Amino acids come from protein.

items.stem: A diagram shows an enzyme with a notch, and three molecules: one with a matching notch shape, one square and one round. Which can the enzyme act on?

figure.alt: One enzyme with a notch-shaped active site and three possible substrates: a matching notched shape, a rectangle and a circle.

options.text: Only the molecule with the matching shape
options.feedback: Its shape is complementary to the active site, so only it can fit in and be broken down.

options.text: All three, but at different speeds
options.feedback: A substrate either fits or it does not. An enzyme has no effect at all on a molecule that cannot enter its active site.

options.text: The square one, because it is the largest
options.feedback: Size is not the test; shape is. The active site and the substrate have to be complementary.

options.text: None, until the enzyme changes shape to fit
options.feedback: In the lock and key model the shape is fixed. A change of shape here is denaturation, which stops the enzyme working altogether.

items.stem: Why must food molecules be digested before they can be used by the body?
items.skill: Give the size-and-solubility reason for digestion

options.text: They are large and insoluble, so they cannot be absorbed into the blood
options.feedback: Large and insoluble in, small and soluble out. Those four words carry the marks.

options.text: They contain too much energy to be absorbed at once
options.feedback: Energy is not the problem. The problem is that the molecules are too big to cross the gut wall.

options.text: They have to be turned into enzymes first
options.feedback: Enzymes do the digesting; they are not what the food becomes.

options.text: They would poison the blood if absorbed whole
options.feedback: Whole food molecules are not poisonous; they simply cannot get through. Answer with size and solubility.

items.stem: A biological washing powder removes blood and grease stains at 40 °C. Which enzymes does it most likely contain?
items.skill: Apply enzyme names to a commercial use

options.text: protease and lipase
options.feedback: Blood is protein, so protease; grease is fat, so lipase. Name the stain first and the enzyme follows.

options.text: amylase and carbohydrase
options.feedback: Those two are the same enzyme group and they work on starch, which is not what either stain is made of.

options.text: amylase only
options.feedback: Amylase would handle a gravy or pasta stain. Blood and grease need protease and lipase.

parts.stem:
Use the words below to label the diagram of stage 1.

active site · enzyme · substrate

scheme.for: enzyme (the larger molecule with the notch)
active site (the notch itself)
substrate (the molecule that fits in)

hints: The active site is a part of the enzyme, not a separate molecule.
There is no product yet at stage 1 — nothing has reacted.
parts.workedSolution: The large molecule with the notch is the enzyme; the notch itself is the active site; the molecule above it, shaped to fit, is the substrate.

commonErrors.feedback: Products only exist after the reaction, at stage 3. At stage 1 the molecule going in is the substrate.

scheme.for: simple sugars / glucose
protein
lipase

hints: Read across each row: the enzyme is named after the substrate, and the products are what comes out.
'Lipid' is a food group; 'lipase' is the enzyme — the ending -ase means enzyme.
parts.workedSolution: Carbohydrase (amylase) turns starch into simple sugars. Protease turns protein into amino acids. Lipase turns fat into fatty acids and glycerol.

commonErrors.feedback: Lipid is the food, lipase is the enzyme. Every digestive enzyme name on this specification ends in -ase.

parts.stem: Explain why this enzyme has no effect on the other two molecules.

scheme.for: their shapes are not complementary to the active site
so they cannot fit into the active site / the enzyme-substrate complex cannot form

commonErrors.feedback: Denaturation is a change to the enzyme caused by heat or pH. Here the enzyme is fine — it is the other molecules whose shape does not match.

parts.stem:

grease is fat, and lipase digests fat
accept: the products are small and soluble so they wash away

hints: Name what each stain is made of first, then the enzyme that works on it.
parts.workedSolution: Blood contains protein, which the protease digests into amino acids; grease is fat, which the lipase digests into fatty acids and glycerol. Both sets of products are small and soluble, so they wash out of the cloth.

commonErrors.feedback: Amylase works on starch, and neither blood nor grease is starch. Match each stain to the food group it belongs to.

reject: it is better for the clothes

context.setting: A small amount of amylase digesting a large volume of starch solution

parts.stem:
A single drop of amylase solution can digest a whole test tube of starch solution.
Explain how this is possible.

accepted: the enzyme is not used up in the reaction so each molecule can act on one substrate molecule after another

scheme.for: the enzyme is not used up / is unchanged by the reaction
so each enzyme molecule can act on one substrate molecule after another
accept: the active site is free again as soon as the products leave

hints: Think about what happens to the active site after the products leave.
parts.workedSolution: An enzyme is a catalyst, so it is not used up in the reaction. As soon as the products leave the active site it is empty again, and the same enzyme molecule can bind the next starch molecule — so a very few enzyme molecules can digest a great many substrate molecules.

commonErrors.feedback: Enzymes do not multiply. The point is that each one is unchanged after every reaction, so it can be used over and over.

context.setting: A lock and key diagram for a reaction that digests starch, with three molecules lettered

figures.alt: Three stages of a reaction. Stage 1: molecule P, with a notch in its surface labelled active site, and molecule Q above it. Stage 2: Q sitting in the notch of P. Stage 3: P as it was before, and the two halves of Q leaving as two molecules, R.

parts.stem:
In the diagram, molecule **P** has the active site, molecule **Q** fits into it and molecule **R** is released at the end. The reaction digests starch.
Choose the **two** terms in the list that describe molecule **P**.

enzyme · substrate · product · amylase · starch · simple sugar · lipase · amino acid

scheme.for: enzyme
amylase (accept carbohydrase)

hints: One word for its job, one for its name.
Only one enzyme on the list digests starch.
parts.workedSolution: P has the active site and is unchanged at the end, so its job is enzyme. The reaction digests starch, so its name is amylase.

commonErrors.feedback: Lipase works on fat and protease on protein. The stem says the reaction digests starch, which fixes the enzyme as amylase.

parts.stem: Choose **two** terms from the same list that apply to molecule **Q**.

scheme.for: substrate
starch

hints: Q goes into the active site, so it is what the enzyme acts on.
Amylase acts on starch and turns it into simple sugars — one of those is the substrate and one is the product.
parts.workedSolution: Q fits into the active site, so its job is substrate, and the substrate of amylase is starch.

commonErrors.feedback: Q goes in, so it is the substrate, not the product. Its name is therefore starch rather than a simple sugar.

parts.stem: Choose **two** terms from the same list that apply to molecule **R**.

scheme.for: product
simple sugar (accept glucose)

hints: R is released at the end, so it is what comes out.

parts.workedSolution: R is released at the end, so its job is product, and the product of amylase acting on starch is a simple sugar such as glucose.

commonErrors.feedback: R comes out of the reaction, so it is a product. Starch is what went in.

parts.stem: Explain why molecule R can be absorbed into the bloodstream but molecule Q cannot.

accepted: R is small and soluble while Q is large and insoluble

Q is large and insoluble, so it cannot
scheme.examinerNote: A comparison is required: both molecules must be described.

hints: Describe both molecules — a comparison needs both halves.
parts.workedSolution: R is a simple sugar: small and soluble, so it passes through the gut wall into the blood. Q is starch: large and insoluble, so it cannot get through until it has been digested.

commonErrors.feedback: Only one of the two molecules has been described. CCEA's schemes ask for comparisons about both things being compared, so say what Q is like as well as R.

the products of starch digestion are simple sugars such as glucose

hints: Two foods, two enzymes, two sets of products — then one paragraph about size and solubility.

parts.workedSolution: Enzymes are proteins that work as biological catalysts: they speed up reactions without being used up. The starch in the toast is digested by carbohydrase, also called amylase, into simple sugars such as glucose. The fat in the butter is digested by lipase into fatty acids and glycerol. Each enzyme works only on its own substrate, because the substrate fits the active site and their shapes are complementary. Starch and fat are large, insoluble molecules and cannot pass through the gut wall, but the simple sugars, fatty acids and glycerol are small and soluble, so they are absorbed into the bloodstream.

commonErrors.feedback: Denaturation is the next topic and it is not what this question asked. Summer 2023's report singles out enzyme answers that include everything the candidate knows; only points that answer the question are counted.

findTheMistake.stem:
Dara is asked: 'The diagram shows an enzyme reaction that digests protein. Molecule X has the active site and molecule Y fits into it. Give two terms that apply to molecule Y. [2]'
His answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Y fits into the active site, so it is what goes in: the substrate. The product is what comes out afterwards. Because the job was wrong, the name went wrong too — the substrate of a protease is protein, and amino acids are its products.
findTheMistake.feedback: Neither mark, and the two errors are really one: the job decides the name. Fix the job first by asking what the molecule is doing in the picture — going in, or coming out — and the name follows from the row of the table. Summer 2025's report says candidates found identifying these terms difficult on exactly this kind of six-mark item.
